items.question: How do you understand the reductionist approach to physics?
items.object: The reductionist approach to physics
items.answer: The reductionist approach is kind of the traditional way we've done physics. It's kind of the very rational, old-school way to do things, which is like, oh, I want to have a model, maybe it's an equation, some analytic model, and it has a few parameters. I've reduced all of physics to a very simple model with few parameters, and ideally the least amount of parameters possible, you know, Occam's razor principle. These equations with these few parameters allow me to have predictive power over the world, and with this predictive power I can steer the world, I can do things, right? I could predict and control it, and that's the goal of physics: to have better models of the world.

items.question: Why do you see a complex systems approach as the way forward for physics?
items.object: The complex systems approach to physics
items.answer: I guess I got swept up in the school of thought that was a generalization of Wheeler's it from bit, which was the it from qubit program, which was seeking to unify theoretical physics through quantum information theory, right? So viewing everything in the universe as one big quantum computer running a certain program or self-simulation. That framework's actually a really useful kind of unifying framework to understand all sorts of systems, and people were studying systems that have some connections between quantum gravity and regular quantum mechanics, in the context of holography. So, AdS/CFT for those that are familiar. But what I realized there was that even whether or not AdS/CFT was going to work, it was clear that the complex systems approach to physics was the way forward. The universe is very complex. Even beyond quantum gravity, just looking at condensed matter systems, you can have equations describing the microscopics, but you can't predict the emergent properties, right? You actually have to apply an amount of computation that is similar to that of the universe to have a prediction of what happens at a larger scale, right? Not all equations you can renormalize analytically. Renormalize means get an effective physics at a larger, more coarse-grained scale. That's how we go from different types of physics, from quantum field theory to quantum theory to statistical mechanics and then eventually classical Newtonian mechanics, and then even beyond that we get to general relativity and so on. So clearly the way forward was to understand everything as a complex system. But that was a sort of ego death because the human can't necessarily be the hero of the story. The model is no longer interpretable. If you have something like a deep learning system—back then we were looking at tensor networks, which are a different sort of parametric complex system that we used to model, let's say, condensed matter systems or quantum gravity systems—if you look at these systems, they're no longer interpretable. I have these big networks and they're just as opaque as the system that I was trying to predict. But with numerics and with a lot of compute, you're leveraging a programmable parametric complex system to grok a complex system of nature for you. In a way, it was like, okay, well, maybe I can't be the hero of the story. I won't be the one to figure out the grand unifying theory of physics, but maybe I could build a computer or computer software that can understand the universe or chunks of the universe for us. The more I dug into it, it was clear that this was going to be the way forward.

items.question: How did trying to understand quantum mechanical systems shape your conception of intelligence?
items.object: Intelligence as learning representations of quantum systems
items.answer: At the time, I came at it trying to understand quantum mechanical systems. So you had systems that have quantum complexity, and there you can show that actually classical representations will struggle to capture quantum correlation. So already, I came at it from a non-anthropomorphic form of intelligence. To me, intelligence was just—I'm trying to learn compressed representations of systems through parameterized distributions, or in my case it was parameterized wave functions and density matrices, which is the more general form. Initially it was mostly numerics with tensor networks. But there was another institute I was part of at University of Waterloo, the Institute for Quantum Computing. There it was very interesting because we had these controllable quantum systems. We had these control parameters, and it became clear to me that there was maybe a way to run these representations we were trying to learn of quantum systems that are parametric on a parametric programmable quantum system. So now we could fight fire with fire. We can have parametric quantum complexity that's tunable to understand quantum complexity of our world, right? And that's actually my entry into artificial intelligence. I wrote up some of the first algorithms for quantum neural networks. That's what we called them. They have nothing to do with actual neurons. They're just parameterized quantum programs.

items.question: How do you distinguish physics-based computing from digital emulations of physics-inspired algorithms?
items.object: Physics-based computing
items.answer: Yeah, I mean a quantum computer is a computer that leverages quantum mechanical evolutions as a resource. There's more formal definitions of what a quantum computer is, but a physics-based computer, of course, like every physical thing is embedded in the physical universe, so everything is physics-based. But it is true that it's kind of a continuum, right? Because you can have physics-inspired computers that are doing digital emulations of physics-inspired algorithms. I would say that's physics-inspired. I would say a physics-based computer, at least for a quantum mechanical computer, is one where you have a sort of parameterized Schrödinger evolution that you control, and you can show that it has some unitarity. And then in our case, we're building physics-based stochastic computers or stochastic thermodynamic computers. They're parameterized stochastic evolutions that we control. In principle, you could try to emulate a quantum mechanical computer, emulate a stochastic computer digitally. Of course, in the case of a quantum mechanical computer, there's proven separations of complexity there, and there's experiments showing that you can't emulate them at scale. In our case, with stochastic computers there's no complexity class separation; it's just orders-of-magnitude constant speedup or energy-efficiency gain, which practically makes them intractable to emulate at scale. Not impossible, though, of course.

items.question: What led you to move from quantum computing toward thermodynamic computing?
items.object: The move from quantum computing to thermodynamic computing
items.answer: Going from being one of the first programmers of AI on quantum computers and seeing the field evolve over several years—I mean, I was almost eight years in quantum computing—it wasn't progressing as fast as I wanted. I was seeing a sort of writing on the wall where, to have a quantum mechanical computer, you try to keep the computer at perfect zero temperature, zero entropy. So you're constantly pumping out entropy that's seeping into the system through noise, right? And that's quantum error correction and fault tolerance. It turns out that most of your computation, most of your energy, is going to be sunk into that pumping. So it's like an algorithmic form of refrigeration. To me it's like, if you have a fridge and you're trying to keep your freezer really cold, it's going to use up a lot of energy if the rest of the room is at room temperature, because that gradient of temperature is very difficult to maintain. So it's like, okay, what if we had a hotter physics-based computer? Maybe it'd be much easier to maintain. Just the first thought, right? And so what would that look like? In the limit where you let the noise seep in, things become mostly stochastic; the quantumness kind of fades out, and we know this from renormalization of physics. That's why we don't have to care so much about quantum physics day to day, because it gets washed out at larger scales, right?

items.question: Why do you think we need to loosen our grip on control in computing, from software to physical hardware?
items.object: Control and uncertainty in computing
items.answer:
The ideal quantum computer has no probabilistic uncertainty. In fact, when there is probabilistic uncertainty, that's when the quantum computer loses its quantum coherence. It becomes non-quantum, right? And we have a very similar problem with classical computers that I realized, which was we use all this power to have signal that's so strong relative to the jitter of electrons and the amplitude of that jitter in order to maintain determinism. We want our transistors to be absolutely on or absolutely off because we have a lot of transistors and we want the computer to be in a deterministic state that we have control over, right? Because humans like to be in control; when we're not in control, there's anxiety. But I think we got to learn to let go, just like I learned to, in a way, let go of control mentally by giving up the reductionist approach, which is the human-interpretable approach to physics.

We have to, just like we did with deep learning, let go of software 1.0, imperative programming, and let gradient descent be a better programmer than you. That was very humbling for some. Some are still trying to hang on for control, with ML interpretability research and all this AI safety research, and they still want to feel like they're in control or that they understand the complex system instead of letting it do its thing and letting it figure out what's best. That's also my main gripe with the whole AI safety field. Of course, there should be some research in interpretability, but I just don't think they're going to go that far. To close the loop here, I think we should also literally let go, loosen our grip on electrons and hardware. That's what we do: essentially, we go from having a very tight grip and yanking these signals around to loosening our grip, letting there be fuzz and gently guiding the signals. In some sense you're switching teams. In the more classical way of thinking of this, what we're trying to do is keep the noise at bay, to make our systems as non-stochastic as possible.

items.question: How do you understand the energy advantage of thermodynamic computers over classical or quantum computers?
items.object: The energy advantage of thermodynamic computing
items.answer: Reducing entropy in a system, keeping something in a deterministic state, always costs you energy. If every clock cycle we're trying to prevent the classical or quantum computer from decaying to a naturally probabilistic and relaxed thermal state, then we have to pay the price. We have to pay energy to maintain determinism and reduce entropy. Whereas a thermodynamic computer is not always at equilibrium, but we're dancing much closer to equilibrium, and it's much cheaper energetically to sit in those states and maintain those states, right?

items.question: How do you approach combining stochastic physics with deterministic computation in your thermodynamic computing chips?
items.object: The design of thermodynamic computing chips as Markov chain Monte Carlo accelerators
items.answer: For a technical audience, I guess they're Markov chain Monte Carlo accelerators, right? We support discrete variables, continuous variables, mixtures of the two. Essentially we've found a way to harness natural stochastic physics of electrons in order to accelerate Markov chain Monte Carlo. There's some subtleties on how we do that mapping, but you could just imagine we're embedding our continuous or discrete variable MCMC into the stochastic dynamics that are parametric and that we have control over those parameters. We're embedding them into the dynamics of the electrons in the device. It is partly analog. It is stochastic, but our most recent chip is a mixed-signal chip. So we use digital classical components and stochastic electronics, and the two have to interact, just like in a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. You have some components of the algorithm that have some entropy, some proposals, and then you have some non-random parts, like computing acceptance or rejection.

items.question: How do you understand the role of probabilistic computation in today's AI workloads?
items.object: Probabilistic computation in contemporary AI
items.answer:
You could think of even a transformer: you have a softmax layer at the end. A transformer is a big probabilistic computer already. So we're running probabilistic software on this stack that was made for determinism. That's highly inefficient. And now with test-time compute, thinking at test time, Monte Carlo research and all sorts of RL rollouts, that's a Monte Carlo algorithm, right? That can be tree of thoughts, discrete diffusion, and now even for content there's diffusion models. Those are also a Markov chain; you're reversing a Markov chain there.

The biggest workloads that are eating the world and consuming a ton of energy are actually probabilistic workloads. They are probabilistic graphical models. It's kind of funny; I think it's just the community. The new additions to machine learning that don't learn the fundamentals just go straight to transformers or whatever is hot. And then I tell them we're building an accelerator for probabilistic graphical models, and they look at me like, what are you talking about? items.question: How do you understand the thermal danger zone as a limit on making deterministic computers smaller?
items.object: The thermal danger zone as a limit on scaling deterministic computers
items.answer: I mean, I came from quantum computing. If you try to scale up your system, you have noise seep in. You're going from the quantum zone of physics to the thermodynamic; you're edging on it. And then if you're in the classical zone but you try to get smaller, then you're getting in the thermal zone again, in terms of the physics and the jitter of electrons, because your transistors are so small. The fact that there's very few electrons, and the transistors are small, the jitter of the electron population matters compared to the amplitude of the signal. Typically we like our computers to have an error rate of 10 to the minus 15 so that you can do many operations before there's an error, and so that you don't have to run error correction. The only computers that usually run error correction are those that we send in space because of radiation. The reason we can't scale down deterministic computers is because of this thermal danger zone. They're innovating in all sorts of ways. They're doing all sorts of weird fins and weird designs that are hardware-level error correction.

I would say most things would be well covered by probabilistic and deterministic representations.

items.question: How do you understand effective accelerationism (EAC) as a prescription for civilization's growth?
items.object: Effective accelerationism (EAC)
items.answer: EAC is a sort of metaculture. I call it a cultural hyperparameter prescription, if you will. It's one where we're trying to maximize growth of civilization as measured by our free energy production and consumption, aka the Kardashev scale. The Kardashev scale is a log scale tracking how much free energy is consumed and produced. It comes from the realization, as I was studying stochastic thermodynamics in preparation for founding Extropic, that there was this generalization of Darwinian selection, thermodynamic selection, where each bit—you go from selfish genes to selfish memes to selfish bits. Every bit of information specifying a configuration of matter is fighting for its existence in the future. The selection pressure on those bits of information is whether they can further host organisms' ability to understand their environment, predict the future, capture free energy, use it strategically, and grow. The master metric is: if I change this parameter to this value and let time evolve, how much free energy has a system dissipated through its trajectory over time? The theorems of stochastic thermodynamics tell us that trajectories of the system that consume more free energy are exponentially more likely. That's how you have this pruning of branches that consume less free energy. This is the golden metric of selection pressure on the space of bits. I will design the highest-fitness selfish meme that is EAC: figure out what is optimal for growth and do it. By construction it should be the most viral thing, and it will persist and surprise you.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between the United States and China in how they innovate?
items.object: The United States and China as contrasting approaches to innovation
items.answer: To me that seemed like the main advantage of the United States: it's very high variance. They have high-variance individuals and high-variance outcomes. I view the United States as a high-temperature search algorithm. They're always first to figure things out. They're first to figure things out because they're always searching in very high variance. I view innovation as a diffusion process in some landscape, and they're in a very high-noise regime so they don't get stuck in local optima. China is more like the low-temperature sampler, the optimizer at the end. They're doing the gradient descent once there's consensus, once there's a clear gradient of direction of improvement. It's easy to convince a committee at that point, and then you can execute top-down control with a lot of conviction. They beat us in the final stretch when you have—it's like Bayesian inference. You go from an unsharp prior to a sharper posterior on what's optimal. It's like annealing. China beats us at squeezing the end because they have a lot more top-down control power and a lot more coherence there. I see this as a parallel-tempering algorithm between the United States, the high-temperature search and discovering things first, and China optimizing and improving technologies and scaling manufacturing.

items.question: Why do you worry more about a “1984”-style outcome than AI doom?
items.object: Authoritarian concentration and the loss of exploratory variance
items.answer: For me, P(1984) was higher than P(doom) from AI. To me, China is the ultimate monopolistic company. There's basically one set of executives for all the companies; they're acting like a conglomerate and they throw their weight around to crush American smaller companies. One thing about EAC is that we're anti-monopolistic, because monopolies tend to be suboptimal. If you have choices of hyperparameters that are over-concentrated, you're not exploring anymore. That motivates my worry: very authoritarian forms of government where we impose ethnic or cultural homogeneity are very good at minimizing free energy. What we're arguing for is embracing variance, different cultures, different bets. It could be culture, genetics, or ways to train your ML models.

items.question: How do you understand the risks of centralization in AI research?
items.object: Centralization and reduced variance in AI research
items.answer: There's been some centralization in AI research labs. Even though there are four or five players that matter, they kind of churn. It's been a meme recently that researchers slosh around and churn between each other, so they're all kind of equilibrating in terms of beliefs, because you have exchange of researchers between the labs. You could see that the American research labs all converge to similar amounts of performance at similar compute. China with DeepSeek was exploring a whole different region of hyperparameter space due to its export-control constraints, and then showed us that over-concentrating our bets in hyperparameter space has risks because we're stuck in a local optimum and there might be a better nonlocal global optimum that we're missing. Again, it's just been our push for variance, in order to always be exploring. I think it's really important. It's hard to explain. It's the same pattern that happens in Western governments and late-stage corporations, large bureaucracies: a cover-your-ass mentality and culture, and decision by committee. It tends to be variance-reducing, variance-killing.

items.question: Why do you think maintaining a variety of research bets matters when AI development might be stuck in a local optimum?
items.object: Exploration and variance in AI research investment
items.answer: As long as you don't kill variance completely and you keep some exploration, you're not just purely exploiting; you keep open-mindedness, and you're always spending some resources exploring and potentially finding a better way to do things. Some people at first thought our bet was ludicrous and we shouldn't have raised VC funding. There's trillions of dollars of capital riding on the current paradigm, and you don't want a startup to raise a few tens of millions to take a bet that would be completely disruptive to everything, to this whole multitrillion-dollar bet. Now the tune is changing a lot because people planning these half-a-trillion-dollar buildouts want to know if a technology that's a thousand x better is around the corner, and could render some of their buildouts miscalibrated in terms of the ratio of energy to compute and density.

items.question: How do you see thermodynamic computing fitting into the AI infrastructure being built today?
items.object: Thermodynamic computing's relationship to conventional AI hardware
items.answer: I don't think thermodynamic computing is going to work other than in tandem with GPUs or TPUs or neural processing units. It's going to take quite a while for models to be fully ported to thermodynamic computers. For the foreseeable future, these buildouts are safe, and you could just have thermodynamic computing as an add-on.
